Many packages are available for calculating objective functions (e.g., the R package hydroGOF, Zambrano-Bigiarini 2020) and implementing sensitivity analyses (e.g., the python library SALib, Herman and Usher 2017), but rarely do these packages communicate with one other.
There is a need for future research to integrate existing coding packages within universal workflows for robust hydrologic model analyses.
Our study objective was to develop a welldocumented, adaptable, and reproducible workflow for evaluating hydrologic model parameter sensitivities and uncertainties.
The workflow needed to objectively evaluate model output as a function of parameter choice using both numerical and visualization techniques.

The workflow was developed with the interests of the National Water Center (NWC) and for the National Water Model (NWM) outputs, however, the goal was to develop a modular tool for easy integration into different hydrologic modeling frameworks for objective modular model and parameter scheme evaluations, which provide data useful for model selection.

To our knowledge, how we have implemented this workflow is new and of importance to agencies, like the NWC, and other research groups where models are run with large parameter sets or outputs are evaluated using multiple metrics.

We deconstructed and integrated an existing R package (hydroGOF) and a python sensitivity analysis library (SALib) with new R and python scripts executed within different modules of the resulting workflow.

We tested the workflow using three common hydrologic models: Storm Water Management Model (SWMM; Rossman 2015), Hydrologiska Byrans Vat- ˚ tenbalansavdelning (HBV) model (Bergstrom 1992, ¨ 1995; Seibert and Vis 2012), and TOPMODEL (Beven 1997).
This paper details implementation of the workflow and a sensitivity analysis on eleven input parameters for SWMM-simulated streamflow.

Visualization techniques were included in this paper for one objective function; however, visuals for five additional objective functions are available via our github repository (refer to Supporting Information).
For each case study, an executable Jupyter Notebook with all Python and R scripts was included in the github repository.

The variety in model outputs and objective functions for each case study directly featured the modular nature and reproducibility of our workflow because of the different model inputs, parameter sets, configurations, and outputs.
